title: Terroir and Soil Science
description: Understand Burgundy's complex geological structure, soil types, and how terroir shapes wine style
lessons.0.title: The Concept of Terroir
lessons.0.slides.0.title: The Concept of Terroir
lessons.0.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 1 - 18 minutes
lessons.0.slides.0.description: A deep dive into Burgundy's most fundamental concept: terroir
lessons.0.slides.1.title: What Is Terroir?
lessons.0.slides.1.content: Terroir is a French term encompassing all natural factors that shape a wine's character — soil, climate, topography, microclimate, and more. In Burgundy, even the smallest difference in terroir produces dramatically different wines.
lessons.0.slides.2.title: 🌍 Components of Terroir
lessons.0.slides.2.points.0: Soil — geological structure, mineral composition, drainage
lessons.0.slides.2.points.1: Climate — temperature, rainfall, hours of sunshine
lessons.0.slides.2.points.4: Human factors — viticulture and winemaking (not natural, yet profoundly influential)
lessons.0.slides.3.title: Why Does Burgundy Place Such Importance on Terroir?
lessons.0.slides.3.content: What makes Burgundy unique is this: the same grape variety (Pinot Noir or Chardonnay), the same winemaking technique — yet entirely different wines emerge from different terroirs. Even two adjacent plots can differ dramatically in quality.
lessons.0.slides.4.title: 📍 Three Hallmarks of Burgundy Terroir
lessons.0.slides.4.points.0: Extreme precision — plots (Climat) are delineated with extraordinary fineness
lessons.0.slides.4.points.1: Deep history — monks began studying plot differences in the Middle Ages
lessons.0.slides.4.points.2: Scientific validation — modern soil science has confirmed the accuracy of traditional classifications
lessons.0.slides.4.points.3: Single variety — almost exclusively Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, highlighting terroir differences
lessons.0.slides.4.points.4: Classification system — a strict hierarchy built on terroir quality
lessons.0.slides.5.title: Climat — The Named Plot
lessons.0.slides.5.content: Burgundy has over 1,000 named Climats, each with unique terroir and history. In 2015, Burgundy's Climat system was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List.
lessons.0.slides.6.title: 🏆 Famous Climat Examples
lessons.0.slides.6.points.0: Romanée-Conti — 1.8 ha, world's most expensive wine
lessons.0.slides.6.points.1: Clos de Vougeot — 50 ha, quality varies markedly by position
lessons.0.slides.6.points.4: Every Climat has its own distinct personality
lessons.0.slides.7.title: 🧠 Terroir Concept Quiz
lessons.1.title: Geological Structure and Soil Types
lessons.1.slides.0.title: Geological Structure and Soil
lessons.1.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 2 - 20 minutes
lessons.1.slides.0.description: Explore Burgundy's complex geological history and soil types
lessons.1.slides.1.title: Burgundy's Geological History
lessons.1.slides.1.content: Burgundy's soils formed during the Jurassic period approximately 150 million years ago, when this region was a shallow sea. The remains of marine organisms accumulated to form fossil-rich limestone — the bedrock of all Burgundy soils.
lessons.1.slides.2.title: The Three Key Jurassic Limestones of Burgundy
lessons.1.slides.3.title: 🪨 Principal Soil Types
lessons.1.slides.3.points.0: Limestone — the most prevalent; imparts minerality
lessons.1.slides.3.points.1: Marl — limestone + clay; good water retention
lessons.1.slides.3.points.2: Clay — retains water and nutrients; suits Pinot Noir
lessons.1.slides.3.points.3: Gravel — excellent drainage; promotes early ripening
lessons.1.slides.3.points.4: Kimmeridgian — unique to Chablis; rich in oyster fossils
lessons.1.slides.4.title: 🍷 Soil Type and Grape Variety
lessons.1.slides.4.points.1: Marl (limestone + clay) → suited to Pinot Noir (red)
lessons.1.slides.4.points.2: High clay content → fuller body, needs time to age
lessons.1.slides.4.points.3: High limestone content → elegant, pronounced minerality
lessons.1.slides.5.title: Côte de Nuits vs. Côte de Beaune Soils
lessons.1.slides.6.title: The Importance of Soil Depth
lessons.1.slides.6.content: Topsoil (30–60 cm) provides immediate nutrition. Subsoil, reaching several metres deep, governs drainage and mineral uptake. Burgundy's finest sites typically have shallow topsoil over deep subsoil, forcing roots to penetrate deeply.
lessons.1.slides.7.title: 🧠 Geological Structure and Soil Quiz
lessons.2.title: Slope Aspect, Altitude, and Microclimate
lessons.2.slides.0.title: Slope Aspect, Altitude, and Microclimate
lessons.2.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 3 - 17 minutes
lessons.2.slides.0.description: Understand how topography influences wine quality
lessons.2.slides.1.title: The Topography of the Côte d'Or
lessons.2.slides.1.content: The Côte de Nuits and Côte de Beaune together form the 'Côte d'Or' (Golden Slope), a north–south ridge at 250–400 m altitude, facing east or southeast — ideal conditions for viticulture.
lessons.2.slides.2.title: ☀️ The Influence of Aspect
lessons.2.slides.2.points.0: East-facing — morning sun, slow warming, preserves acidity
lessons.2.slides.2.points.1: Southeast-facing — longest sunshine, grapes ripen fully
lessons.2.slides.2.points.2: South-facing — strongest light, useful in cool vintages
lessons.2.slides.2.points.3: West-facing — afternoon sun, warm but can overheat
lessons.2.slides.3.title: ⛰️ The Influence of Altitude
lessons.2.slides.3.points.0: 200–250 m — Regional AOC, flatland or hillfoot
lessons.2.slides.3.points.4: Above 350 m — generally too cold for reliable ripening
lessons.2.slides.3.points.5: Temperature drops ~0.6 °C for every 10 m gained
lessons.2.slides.4.title: The Importance of Gradient
lessons.2.slides.4.content: An ideal gradient of 5–15°: too gentle means poor drainage; too steep makes cultivation difficult. The right gradient ensures drainage, maximises solar exposure, reduces frost risk, and allows natural soil stratification.
lessons.2.slides.5.title: 🌡️ Microclimate Factors
lessons.2.slides.5.points.0: Stone walls (Clos) — retain heat, block wind, reflect sunlight
lessons.2.slides.5.points.1: Woodland — windbreak but may shade vines
lessons.2.slides.5.points.2: Valley floors — cold air pools, higher frost risk
lessons.2.slides.5.points.3: Water bodies — moderate temperature, increase humidity
lessons.2.slides.6.title: A Classic Example: Clos de Vougeot
lessons.2.slides.6.content: The 50-hectare Clos de Vougeot Grand Cru shows a clear quality gradient from top to bottom: upper slope (well-drained, excellent sun exposure) → top quality; mid-slope → very good; lower slope (deeper soils, flatter) → more ordinary. A compelling demonstration of how position on the slope is decisive.
lessons.2.slides.7.title: 🧠 Slope Aspect, Altitude, and Microclimate Quiz
lessons.3.title: Climate Factors and Vintage Variation
lessons.3.slides.0.title: Climate and Vintage
lessons.3.slides.0.subtitle: Lesson 4 - 15 minutes
lessons.3.slides.0.description: Understand how climate shapes Burgundy's vintage-to-vintage variation
lessons.3.slides.1.title: Burgundy's Continental Climate
lessons.3.slides.1.content: Burgundy has a continental climate: four distinct seasons, large temperature swings, and moderate rainfall. This brings superb acidity and aromatics — but also means enormous variation between vintages.
lessons.3.slides.2.title: 🌤️ Conditions for a Great Vintage
lessons.3.slides.2.points.0: Frost-free spring — protecting newly budded vines
lessons.3.slides.2.points.1: Warm, dry summer — healthy vine growth
lessons.3.slides.2.points.3: Dry harvest period — avoiding dilution and rot
lessons.3.slides.2.points.4: Moderate rainfall year-round — neither too much nor too little
lessons.3.slides.2.points.5: Large diurnal temperature swings — preserving acidity and aromatics
lessons.3.slides.3.title: ⚠️ Principal Climate Risks
lessons.3.slides.3.points.1: Hail — can devastate a vineyard in minutes
lessons.3.slides.3.points.2: Excess rain — dilutes concentration, encourages disease
lessons.3.slides.3.points.3: Drought — vine stress halts development (increasingly common)
lessons.3.slides.3.points.4: Excess heat — strips elegance and acidity
lessons.3.slides.4.title: The Impact of Climate Change
lessons.3.slides.4.content: Over the past 30 years, average temperatures in Burgundy have risen by approximately 1.5 °C. Benefits: easier ripening, better-balanced acidity. Challenges: over-ripeness, loss of freshness, increased pest and disease pressure, more frequent extreme weather events.
lessons.3.slides.5.title: 🍇 Vintage Classification
lessons.3.slides.5.points.3: Difficult vintages (e.g. 2013, 2021) — frost or excessive rain
lessons.3.slides.5.points.4: Top producers make fine wine even in difficult vintages
lessons.3.slides.6.title: Terroir vs. Vintage
lessons.3.slides.6.content: Terroir is the fixed geography; vintage is the variable climate. Great terroir (Grand Cru) in a difficult year still outperforms ordinary terroir in a great year. This is precisely why Grand Cru is always worth the investment.
